video_title: Kenny Smith, NBA Champ tells untold MJ stories, Inside the NBA secrets and life lessons| The Pivot

quotes.speaker: Kenny Smith
quotes.summary_phrase: Kenny Smith on breaking the 3-point record in the Finals
quotes.excerpt: I broke the NBA record at that time for threes in a Final.
quotes.quote: I couldn't go anywhere without people talking about the threes. I broke the NBA record at that time for threes in a Final. Regular season you make your name, the playoffs are when you make your fame.

quotes.speaker: Kenny Smith
quotes.summary_phrase: Kenny Smith on Michael Jordan's unique player development
quotes.excerpt: He's the only player who came into the league where his weaknesses when he left the league were his strengths.
quotes.quote: If you look at him from his day one to his day last, he's the only player who came into the league where his weaknesses when he left the league were his strengths.

quotes.speaker: Kenny Smith
quotes.summary_phrase: Kenny Smith on Michael Jordan's Finals record and hypothetical 8 straight championships
quotes.excerpt: I love the fact that he went to the Finals six times and never lost.
quotes.quote: I love the legacy of Michael. I love the fact that he went to the Finals six times and never lost. But do you really believe, honestly, he would have won eight championships in a row?

quotes.speaker: Kenny Smith
quotes.summary_phrase: Kenny Smith on his broadcasting contract being more than his playing contract
quotes.excerpt: My last one-year contract was more than my first whole NBA contract.
quotes.quote: My last one-year contract was more than my first whole NBA contract. I get paid more to talk about the game than play the game? Like, are you serious?

quotes.speaker: Kenny Smith
quotes.summary_phrase: Kenny Smith on walking off the set of Inside the NBA in 2020
quotes.excerpt: Everything felt normal. I'm like, shit, everything ain't normal? This is not normal.
quotes.quote: All of those voices were in my head. Everything felt normal. I'm like, shit, everything ain't normal? This is not normal. Sometimes not speaking is bigger than speaking. They forget what you say, but they always ask you when you don't say nothing.

quotes.speaker: Kenny Smith
quotes.summary_phrase: Kenny Smith on being known more for broadcasting than playing
quotes.excerpt: Most people, they know me from broadcasting and not from playing.
quotes.quote: It's funny because most people, they know me from broadcasting and not from playing. Most people have not seen me play. When I hear guys talk about eras of basketball, I always laugh because I know for a fact, they've never seen me play, ever. Never in their life. So they're talking about things that they're really just watching clips of and not watching the totality or the moments. When they evaluate players, evaluate things, evaluate anything, I know they didn't see me play, their evaluation sometimes...

quotes.speaker: Kenny Smith
quotes.summary_phrase: Kenny Smith on his career perception and breaking the 3-point record
quotes.excerpt: Regular season you make your name, the playoffs are when you make your fame.
quotes.quote: In my first five to seven years, I couldn't go anywhere without people talking about the threes. I broke the NBA record at that time for threes in a Final. You get measured. Regular season you make your name, the playoffs are when you make your fame. So you're doing it on the biggest stage. You're breaking the NBA record. So it was talked about. People shouldn't kind of remember it because greatness really to me is not moments, it's also the extent of how long you do it.

quotes.speaker: Kenny Smith
quotes.summary_phrase: Kenny Smith on his 'shit talker' nature and Michael Jordan's competitive response
quotes.excerpt: This all day, I'm in his ear and he's talking and all day, we're just going back and forth.
quotes.quote: I'm a shit talker. But he did it and he had some things to do with it. So I just enjoyed being in that environment. He was that he was a guy. When I saw The Last Dance and people were like, 'Oh, he was so hard.' I'm like, 'Man, that's what I loved about it.' I loved the fact that, you know, we just all day and he's like, he's just all day, I'm in his ear and he's talking and all day, we're just going back and forth. I love that part. I love the, 'Yo, if you don't come to play today,' you know, that, I love that. That got me, that's the way I grew up.

quotes.speaker: Kenny Smith
quotes.summary_phrase: Kenny Smith on being jealous of Scottie Pippen
quotes.excerpt: For my first six years I was always jealous of Scottie Pippen.
quotes.quote: I don't think I've ever said this, for my first six years I was always jealous of Scottie Pippen. I was so jealous because I was the sixth pick, he was the fifth. I visited Chicago. They brought me in on an interview. I was so jealous because I was like, I knew what he could do and bring out of you. You always have it in you, but you sometimes you need somebody to elevate it to another level. And I knew that he would do that. So I used to look at Scottie and be so jealous of that. You forget the first three, four years in Chicago, Scottie had the migraines. He wasn't Scottie Pippen until about his third, fourth year. My first three years, I was Kenny Smith. I was first team All-Rookie. I'm having 17, 18 points a game as a second-year guy on a bad team where I'm the number one option on a bad team.

quotes.speaker: Kenny Smith
quotes.summary_phrase: Kenny Smith on why the Bulls lost to Orlando in 1995
quotes.excerpt: If Horace Grant was still with them, they would have beat Orlando.
quotes.quote: The only reason I always say we would have beat them, and I'm glad we didn't face them, because I love the legacy of Michael. I love the fact that he went to the Finals six times and never lost. I love that legacy. I wouldn't have wanted to be part of that. But do you really believe, honestly, he would have won eight championships in a row? The one thing that I always thought why we could beat them the second year was they were too small. Horace Grant had already went to Orlando and Dennis Rodman wasn't there. That's the reason they lost to Orlando. If Horace Grant was still with them, they would have beat Orlando. But the fact that he was gone, they became such a smaller team and we had Hakeem Olajuwon. If you're not double teaming Hakeem Olajuwon, you cannot beat us because we splash you up too much from three. They had no one could guard Hakeem Olajuwon. They would have been playing him one-on-one. They were just too little. And then when they got Rodman, they went on that next run. That's all he needed. He needed some size, some defensive intensity on the back end.

quotes.speaker: Kenny Smith
quotes.summary_phrase: Kenny Smith on the Rockets' undying confidence in the playoffs
quotes.excerpt: We might lose, but it ain't going to be tonight.
quotes.quote: Our motto, I used to, game right before Game 5 or Game 7, I'd be like, 'We might lose, but it ain't going to be tonight.' And then we go out. I always say that, the last thing I would say, because I just felt that no one could beat us in that game. Not in a game, but in that game, because we had from Sam Cassell and Mario Elie, guys who are underrated in what they did. Robert Horry was at that time was playing like Scottie Pippen. I just felt we'd never lose. I didn't think anybody could beat us in that game. The game that mattered. At that time, I think we had went like six games in a row close-out games where we didn't lose. They just couldn't close us out. We just had something. We played better on the road, which was weird. We played much better on the road. We united. It was just like, it was a different feeling. Being on the road was so uniting and so galvanizing. That's the thing I remember most about the relationship with my teammates.

quotes.speaker: Kenny Smith
quotes.summary_phrase: Kenny Smith on Dean Smith asking what he's doing for the Black race
quotes.excerpt: He was the first white person that ever asked me, 'What am I doing for the Black race?'
quotes.quote: Dean Smith's first conversation to me was when I was a freshman. He brings me in the office and his first conversation he says to me, 'Kenny, what are you going to do for African Americans on this campus?' Because it was the during the time of Mandela being in prison. We had shanties on campus. He said, 'And if you decide to ever miss campus, miss class or practice because you want to participate in that, you're welcome to.' He was the first white person that ever asked me, 'What am I doing for the Black race?'

quotes.speaker: Kenny Smith
quotes.summary_phrase: Kenny Smith on the success of Inside the NBA
quotes.excerpt: We were really good before Chuck came and Chuck just threw gasoline on the fire.
quotes.quote: I'm going to say it, and this is not offensive, but we created what the podcast world is now. Because the way we behaved allowed people to have more of a freedom of speech. And that's what I always loved about Chuck. We were really good before Chuck came and Chuck just threw gasoline on the fire. Chuck has allowed people to see a different side of me because now I get asked questions that I never got asked before. Because he was one of those guys in the locker room, they'd be like, 'Okay, you had 20 points tonight.' And then they talk about that. And then they'd go, 'What about George Floyd?' He was the only guy in the locker room they would ask. They wouldn't ask other guys. So now he's with me. So they're like, 'George Floyd, Martha Stewart.' We could go all over the place. Now, as you know, you have opinions, thoughts, perspectives on everything in life. You're a citizen of the country just like everybody else is. But they never asked you. They wouldn't ask you when you're in the locker room, how many political questions you get asked? None. But sitting next to Chuck, then it started rolling.

quotes.speaker: Kenny Smith
quotes.summary_phrase: Kenny Smith on individual skill vs. team concepts in the NBA
quotes.excerpt: The individual skills are better at times. The team concepts are not.
quotes.quote: The individual skills are better at times. The team concepts are not. I think because everyone has the individual trainers and they train singularly, they really know how to get their own shot. They're tough shot makers. Things that used to be tough shots are easy shots for guys today. But basketball is also played from the neck up. So the reads are not as smart. That's the only thing I see. That's why the eras are hard to compare, but it's easy to say that both eras could play against each other. Because the reads that they make, they don't have to in this era because they allow you to have eight to nine seconds with the ball instead of pass and move and get off the ball. So most players today just don't know how to play off the ball. They know how to stand in the corner and wait, but they don't know how to play off the ball. They don't know when to cut, they don't know when to go help. But in terms of individual skill set, tough shot makers. They are the tough shot makers. They are the, you know, what the Globetrotters would do. They could do that on a regular. They were, they are tough shot makers. Not more athletic, which is what you hear all the time. Not really. Give me a two guard who's more athletic today than Clyde Drexler. Larry Nance's son isn't as athletic as Larry Nance. His son's in the league and he's not as, so it's not more athleticism, it's more individual work. The casual basketball player that you go to the gym, they're more athletic. That's all it is. They're, you know what I mean? The guy who's in the, when we walked, growing up, when I did, because you're still younger than I am, but when I grew up, if you had a six pack and you weren't playing a sport, you were like, 'What are you doing?' What are you spending three hours in a gym for, bro? You don't play nothing? You could go to any gym right now, any LA Fitness, any Equinox, and be like, 'They don't play nothing. They just work out.' That's my point. So it's just a different era. The casual person is more athletic. The athlete is the same. I think you saw that too, though. I was looking at some of those, the NBA combine numbers. They were just comparing verticals and different things to offensive linemen and football players. The athleticism or the measurables aren't any different, but like you said as well, we watch a dude dribble between his legs 18 times, take 16 steps to step back and we're like, 'Oh, that player is more athletic than Michael Jordan was.' That's actually not the truth for people who understand what they're watching. The skill set is and what's vogue is different. What's vogue. It's not the same. So it's not measurable in that thing, but they are tough shot makers. I will agree with that. They do hit tough shots on more regularity than the players in our era. But they do not play better at times. They also flop. Big ass LeBron James, 6'8", 260, flies into the third row if somebody flips him in his wrist. We all have theatrics. Dennis Rodman was the king of flopping and going all over the floor. Any advantage you can get, you're going to get. Flopping is like an art, honestly. It didn't become called flopping, it was like drawing a foul. But then when they changed the flop, it had a negative connotation. But, 'Yo, you're in the penalty. Figure out a way to get to the line.' They're in the penalty. This 50-50 call can change the dynamic of the game. I'm doing it. It's all about win and loss. Shaq doesn't like flopping because he could just run through people. He doesn't want you falling out because if you're talking strength on strength, he wins. Sometimes we got to jab in the stomach. You can't hit you in the face all the time. He's the Mike Tyson of basketball. Knockout blows.

quotes.speaker: Kenny Smith
quotes.summary_phrase: Kenny Smith on the people who influenced him and seeing greatness
quotes.excerpt: I've always had the ability to see greatness before they became great.
quotes.quote: I think my biggest pivot, it's a combination. It's the people that I've been around and that influenced me. I was writing a book, about halfway through, and I sent in some stuff and the editor goes, 'Do you realize everybody that you, because it was about the people who made me.' It was a tell-all book, everybody who influenced me, but what they did positively to influence me. He's like, 'You realize everybody on your list has a book written about them?' They all have a book. So I was like, 'Really?' So it's the people. From sports, obviously Dean Smith, Michael Jordan, Hakeem Olajuwon. Bill Russell was my first coach. Bill Russell, we, so he had a rule, I had to sit next to him on every plane ride and every bus ride as a rookie. He would talk and he'd say stuff like, 'Yeah, so, you know, Kenny, back in our day, when you know, I was with, you know, me and Malcolm X would go over here and we go eat.' I'm like, 'Malcolm X?' He's like, 'Yeah, Malcolm X.' He would like, 'Yeah, Martin Luther King Jr.' He would tell me stories about them like they were, it was so casual. The people who made me, like him. My college roommate, one of my college roommates, in one summer was a guy named David Kohler. If you look at any plumbing, you're going to see Kohler on it. Nine billion dollars later. College roommate. Didn't pay rent. So we're sitting one night and we're talking about life. He told me, he says, 'You know, my dad would always,' I said, 'You're rich.' He's like, 'Oh, you know,' he's playing it off. I'm like, 'Well, now, so you're just going to take over your father's company?' He's like, 'No. I have to be a plumber first.' I said, 'A plumber?' He says, 'Yeah, because then if someone brings into me and say, 'Okay, this screw is eight dollars.' He's like, 'No, it's not. It's four. I was a plumber. I know what it is.' So I know everything about the business. That's how a point guard thinks. I know everything when when a player, my my center's doing, I have to know where the center's doing, the point guard, the shooting guard, I know everybody's position and play. I just don't know the play, I know what everyone's doing in the play. So we had a kinship and talking. So people like everybody's kind of taking a pivot. Dean Smith with the story about, 'What are you doing for African Americans?' Something that changes your, like, just turns your volume up. I've always had the ability to see greatness before they became great. I would see people and go, 'You're going to be great, man.' And then they turn out to be this, you know. I knew that when I met Kohler. I knew that when I met Guy Oseary, who manages Madonna, Sting. He's like the biggest guy in tech and multi-billionaire. Dude was sleeping on my couch. I was like, 'Bro, you're going to be great.' He's like, 'Man, you know what? I'm not saying I'm not saying that I influenced, but I said, 'You're going to be great.' He said, 'You're the first person ever to say that to me.' Michael B. Jordan, I met on the plane when he was. I'm sitting next to him before he's Michael B. Jordan. He had not had one part yet. So I'm sitting next, talking to this kid and he's like, and he's laughing because his name is Michael B. Jordan. So that's the whole our conversation kicker. I give him my number and about a year later he calls me, he's like, 'Hey, man, I'm moving to LA full-time. If I need a meal, just let me know. If you could, if you got me.' And I go, 'Michael, you'll never need a meal from me. You have it.' He said, 'Really?' That was it. It's something I'm able to see. In the same way with players, Kevin Durant. I was the first to say he's going to be the MVP of the league. They laughed at me. If you look it up and get the clip, Chuck and Chris Webber laughed. 'Kevin Durant, MVP? Never.' I said when I saw Victor Wembanyama, I said in four years, Victor Wembanyama will be in the, three years, I said in four years, Victor Wembanyama will be the MVP of the league, the first time I saw him. They were like, 'No way.' It's all right. It's just something about the greatness, it's not hard to see. For me it isn't. It's like, 'Man.' Sometimes I can take it to myself, but I can definitely see it in other people.
